work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: Homilia de Noe et de arca

paragraphs.text: Now the most holy fast has reached the midpoint of its sacred labours. Now it presses on toward the very height of its toil, toward the arena of the blessed contests. For the middle may certainly be called the peak. For soldiers, the peak is the middle of the war. For those sailing on the sea, the peak of danger is the middle of the struggle and of the storm. The very middle of a human lifetime is youth. The sun is at its strongest in the very middle of the day. So too the peak of the holy days is the very middle of the fast. Where the middle is at its peak, there God dances in the midst. That is why he says: "Be strong, says the Lord, and let the hands of your people be strong; I stand among you, and my Spirit stands in your midst."

So the most holy fast is at its peak, now that it has reached the very middle of its labours. Just as the sun sends out hot rays at the very middle of the day, so the fast too sends out its own bright rays.

The rays of the fast are the divine Scriptures. They give us light, they make our thinking bright, and they set down for us the histories of the ancients, not to praise those who have departed but to rouse those who follow after them to imitate them.

Today, in the middle of the fast, it was read to us how God rescued Noah from the midst of the flood: Noah the marvellous, who swam clear of that agonising ruin and destruction. Just as he had no share with the sinners, so he did not perish with them when they were punished. The flood came to wipe out those who had sinned, and God washed away sin with water. But then he destroyed both the sin and the sinners with water, whereas now grace has been brought in instead, washing away sins with water and at the same time saving sinners. The flood came upon the world at that time to quench the ungodliness that was overflowing in it.

Noah found favour above all others, not because he had some strange nature but because he was found to have a strange will. He shared a common nature with everyone, but his way of life was his own, unlike anyone else's. He lived among them yet mingled with none, sojourning in the world while keeping to his own ways. And standing at the very summit of righteousness, he too receives the calling to be

an image of Christ. Just as Jacob, as was shown last time, lived out the story in the body while tracing out the image of the Saviour in the spirit, so Noah too became a type of the Saviour. But before setting out these insights, I must bring forward the Saviour as a witness, since he took Noah as an image of his own coming. For he says: "As in the days of Noah they were marrying and giving in marriage, and the flood came and swept them all away, so it will be at the coming of the Son of Man." Do you see how he puts the type first and then brings in the truth? In what way, then, is Noah a type of the Saviour? Noah himself builds the ark, he himself lived in the ark, and he came out of the ark; and his own work was his mother. For the ark he had fashioned became his mother. And see the wonder of it. He builds the ark over many years, but he is carried by the ark for a single year. The Saviour prepared the Virgin over many years, yet he was carried by the Virgin in her womb for not even a whole year. Have you seen the shining image of Christ? Take another image of him as well.

In Noah's ark four-footed beasts, creeping things and birds, the whole ordered world, were shut in under his care, all creation together with him. So too with the Saviour: he is born of a virgin and carried in a virgin's womb, yet he holds under his rule things in heaven, things on earth and things under the earth. For the ark was a type both of the Virgin and of the Church. And just as then, in the flood, anyone outside the ark could not live, so now too whoever is outside the Church cannot live. Great is the ark, and it has a second and a third storey, because to him every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth.

But let us come to the story itself. God saw sin overflowing on the earth, and he says to Noah: "Make yourself an ark for salvation, and make the ark of wood that does not rot." The command was short and the work was easy. Yet he spends many years building the ark, not because it needed so much time, but because God, the lover of humankind, was putting off the punishment as he waited for repentance. For sin did not condemn the world so much as the ark did, built and not believed. How was it that they did not lament when they sinned? But even when they saw the ark being built, they did not shudder. We too are punished, not only because we sin, but because we do not quench sin with repentance. The apostle says that the ark condemned the world. So it was not sin that condemned the world, but the ark, because it did not frighten people or alarm them. This is what condemned the world: not that they sinned, but that the threat of punishment did them no good.

For a hundred years Noah too was preaching, not with his tongue but with adze, drill and saw; lifeless tools cried out. Who would not have asked Noah, "What is this structure for? What does this broad ark mean?" And he would have answered: "God, who gives the command, has threatened a flood. He has announced destruction for the world. That is why I am doing this, so that I may be saved." If they had been sensible, they would have said, "The ark is small compared with the threat," and, "What room will there be for us with you?" If they had asked this, they would have quenched God's anger and reaped the salvation that comes from repentance. But they despised Noah. Think of their laughter too. Some mocked Noah and said, "So many years have passed since the flood was threatened!" Do not hurry past the meaning just because the words go by quickly. Think what it was like for a hundred years to ride past while the threat was nowhere fulfilled. Noah was not laughed at as a fool, nor as a man who had lost even ordinary good sense, but because so much time had passed since the flood was threatened.

This is what the Church suffers now at the hands of the enemies of godliness: "Ever since the Christians said, 'The kingdom has drawn near, it is coming,' so many years have passed and nothing has come into view." But Noah endured reproach, and the enemies of godliness went on laughing. Yet they received destruction as the end of their laughter, and he received salvation as the reward for the reproach. "For your name's sake I have borne reproach." And what did God do? When he saw that the time had run its full course and repentance had not come, he says to Noah: "Go in, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives." Do you see the modesty, the rule of self-control? Since there was to be no union of husband and wife in the ark, and husband and wife were not to know the laws of nature, he separates male from female, placing each on its own side, when he says: "Go in, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives." But when he calls him out after the flood, since there was now need for union, for bearing children and for filling the world again, he says: "Go out, you and your wife and your sons and your sons' wives," and so leads them on to bearing children and increasing. And at once, to show that he is moving them to the desire for children, he adds: "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth."

The flood of waters passed (for I must be brief), and the ark comes to rest on the tops of the mountains, for it was an image of the Church. Of the Church the prophet said: "In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be plain to see, and the house of God on the tops of the mountains." Noah came out, having swum clear of the common ruin: the builder of the great vessel, the pilot of the great ship, who inside was carried bodily by the ark, but outside carried the ark by his righteousness. The ark went on, lifted high above the waters, floating and not sinking, tossed by the waves but not swallowed by the deep. This is what the Church suffers now: it is troubled but not destroyed, drenched on every side by the waves of heretics, but steered by the wise Pilot. The ark was an image of the Church. Now a new ark has come in, the Church, and a water that floods away not sinners but sin.

Recently we heard that "much water covers the seas, so as to know the Lord." Here turn your own mind to this: how great an evil he opened up [?] for Noah, and how great a trophy he set up against sin, you have heard. And remember the question we took up last time. I know that some, objecting to what we worked through yesterday, thought they were giving us further exercise on the subject in hand. For some said that he touched on the question of Adam, found himself at a loss, and switched to another topic. But you said: "If God knew beforehand that Adam would sin, why did he create him?" For my part, I know that I left the discussion with no gaps, complete, lacking nothing, and fully worked out by true reasoning.

But since some, with the limping of their own understanding before their eyes, thought the argument was deficient, it is necessary to speak again, not to fill out what is ours, but to make up what is lacking in their faith. I know you remember what was said: that when God foreknows, he does not foreknow in part, but takes in everything together in his knowledge. And you were told that God foreknew that Adam would sin; he foreknew that he would fall and would not keep the commandment. But he foreknew his creature without looking at that alone; he also had in mind those who would come after, who were to become fulfillers of the divine law. For God foreknew, as I said before, the beauty of the patriarchs, the flowering of the prophets, the divine teaching of the apostles, the flower of the dispensation, and the countless thousands of the martyrs. Looking to these, he bore with the one who did not keep the law, so that in these the fulfillers of the law might shine out. For it would not be just for the course of those who do right to be cut off because of the foreknowledge of the one who sinned. He foreknew that Adam would sin; he foreknew that Noah would do right. And to show that it was not nature that sinned but the will that turned aside, fruit came straight from Adam bearing witness to nature that it is good: Abel came forth, attested for his righteousness. If the root was bad, how did it bear holy fruit? If nature was evil, how did it blossom with the fruits of godliness? Listen to the Lord saying: "A rotten tree cannot bear good fruit." If nature were evil, it would not have blossomed with so many fruits of righteousness. But from the first righteous man who blossomed, the child received his testimony and the will was exposed. So God does all things foreseeing everything at once. He foreknew that Adam would sin, but he also foreknew that Adam would be the root of all good things. That is why the apostle, wishing to show that the fruits speak in defence of the root, says: "Adam was not deceived, but Eve was deceived and fell into transgression; yet she will be saved through childbearing."

"Could God not have held back the sinner?" someone says. He could, but there is no reward for those who are held back by compulsion. Nebuchadnezzar, once king of the Babylonians, drunk with arrogance and great power, reached such a pitch of madness that he set up an image of himself and forced those made in the image of God to come and worship the image. God, wishing to show that he could not only throw him out of his kingdom but even banish him from his own nature, took away his kingdom and with it his dignity as a rational being. He no longer ate as a rational man, but ate grass like an ox, and the mind of a beast was given to him. God threw him out of power by compulsion, and there is no reward for one who is compelled: he no longer sinned, and he received no reward. For it is one thing to have something taken away by compulsion, and another to be held back by one's own choice.

Again, Pharaoh took Sarah from Abraham, and when he was about to sin against the holy woman, God afflicted Pharaoh with great and grievous afflictions, and the force and constraint of the afflictions held back the wrongdoing. But the tyrant was given no praise for chastity, because his chastity came not from his own choice but from compulsion and scourges. That is why Joseph is rightly celebrated in song: he held himself back from sin by his own choice, because by choice he overcame compulsion. Pharaoh did not touch Sarah, and Joseph did not touch the Egyptian woman. The deed was the same, but the praise was not the same.

So, brothers, there is no reward for compulsion, but all praise belongs to choice. That is why God says: "If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you." He fixed both virtue and vice in willing and not willing, not because it was impossible to rein in the sinner by nature, but because there was no reward for compulsion. He granted praise to choice.

If you are ungrateful to the divine law that does you good, let the law outside convince you. If we do not sin by choice, and sins came from nature, why do the lawgivers of the Romans punish wickedness? Why do they praise and crown those who achieve virtue? For if nature compelled us, and choice did not direct us, the law would be praising the virtuous and punishing sinners for nothing.

We know in ourselves, brothers, that we do wrong willingly, and that when we sin willingly we are not driven by compulsion. Do you want to learn that each of us knows that sins come from choice and not from nature? When your servant sins against you, why do you not say that the wrong comes from fate? Why do you blame someone who is not to blame? No, when your servant sins against you, you punish him as one who sinned by choice. Yet when you sin against God, do you offer the excuse that you were driven by compulsion?

But enough of this. Let the discussion of choice and free will be kept for another time. And what of the fact that God hardened Pharaoh's heart? Many have tangled themselves up in this idea to their ruin, though it was given for the setting right of souls. But above all, let us hold on to this: the fear of God, and peace. Let us receive these words as arrows of righteousness, not lodged in the body but shot into the soul. The arrows of enemies are for destruction, but the arrows of God are for salvation. Do you want to learn that with God even the names of war are peace? Speaking to Noah he says: "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth; never again will I curse the earth. And this is the sign for you: behold, I set my bow in the cloud." See, the bow is a pledge of peace. Think of the overflowing abundance of grace. May we all be counted worthy of it in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom be glory to the Father with the Holy Spirit to the ages of ages. Amen.
